questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Blockers
questions.stem: In this schematic of a parietal cell, one drug class is shown binding the histamine H2 receptor while another is shown acting directly at the pump. What is the mechanism by which the H2 receptor antagonist reduces acid output?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reversible blockade of the H2 receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irreversible covalent inhibition of the H+/K+-ATPase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blockade of the muscarinic M3 receptor

explanation.summary: H2 receptor antagonists reversibly block histamine at the H2 receptor, reducing the cAMP-dependent pathway that activates the proton pump. This is less complete than PPIs, which irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase itself, the final common pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: H2 receptor antagonists reversibly block histamine at the H2 receptor, reducing the cAMP-dependent pathway that activates the proton pump. This is less complete than PPIs, which irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase itself, the final common pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastrin/CCK-B antagonists block a different stimulatory receptor and are not a standard acid-suppressing class.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutralizing luminal acid is how antacids such as calcium carbonate work; they do not reduce acid output.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Irreversible covalent inhibition of the H+/K+-ATPase is the mechanism of proton pump inhibitors, the other drug class shown.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic M3 blockade interrupts vagal acetylcholine signaling to the parietal cell, a different receptor from the histamine H2 receptor.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Blockers
questions.stem: This figure summarizes categories of harm linked to chronic use of the drug class named at top left. Grouping the listed effects (low Ca2+/Mg2+/Fe2+, osteoporosis, B12 deficiency; C. difficile colitis and pneumonia), what underlying pharmacologic change best explains most of these long-term risks?

explanation.summary: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase, raising gastric pH. The persistently low acidity impairs absorption of Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe2+ and vitamin B12 and removes the acid barrier to enteric pathogens, driving increased risk of malabsorption, osteoporosis, C. difficile infection, and pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase, raising gastric pH. The persistently low acidity impairs absorption of Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe2+ and vitamin B12 and removes the acid barrier to enteric pathogens, driving increased risk of malabsorption, osteoporosis, C. difficile infection, and pneumonia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PPIs do not cause parietal cell apoptosis; long-term use tends to cause parietal cell hyperplasia from raised gastrin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Some PPIs inhibit CYP2C19, such as omeprazole with clopidogrel, but this does not explain malabsorption or infection risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PPIs do not chelate cations; mineral malabsorption results from reduced gastric acidity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reversible H2 receptor blockade is the mechanism of H2 blockers, not the drug class whose chronic harms are listed here.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Blockers
questions.stem: This diagram maps the regulation of gastric acid secretion across the cells of the stomach wall. Which cell type is the direct target of the secreted acid-producing signals and physically expresses the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump?

explanation.summary: The parietal cell is the effector cell of gastric acid secretion; it houses the H+/K+-ATPase and responds to acetylcholine (M3), gastrin, and histamine (H2). G cells secrete gastrin, ECL cells release histamine, chief cells secrete pepsinogen, and D cells release somatostatin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The parietal cell is the effector cell of gastric acid secretion; it houses the H+/K+-ATPase and responds to acetylcholine (M3), gastrin, and histamine (H2). G cells secrete gastrin, ECL cells release histamine, chief cells secrete pepsinogen, and D cells release somatostatin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ECL cells release histamine that acts on the parietal cell; they do not house the proton pump.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D cells release somatostatin, which inhibits acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: G cells in the antrum secrete gastrin, which stimulates acid production indirectly and directly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase, not acid.

questions.stem: This schematic depicts a drug blocking the L-type membrane channel, preventing ion entry that would otherwise initiate processes such as muscle contraction, insulin secretion, and gene transcription. In vascular tissue, which therapeutic effect is a direct consequence of this drug action?

explanation.summary: Blocking the L-type Ca2+ channel lowers intracellular calcium in vascular smooth muscle, reducing myosin light-chain phosphorylation and causing relaxation and vasodilation. The other options are the opposite of, or unrelated to, reduced calcium influx.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blocking the L-type Ca2+ channel lowers intracellular calcium in vascular smooth muscle, reducing myosin light-chain phosphorylation and causing relaxation and vasodilation. The other options are the opposite of, or unrelated to, reduced calcium influx.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced calcium entry decreases, not increases, cardiac contractility (negative inotropy), especially with non-dihydropyridines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium channel blockade relaxes smooth muscle, so it would not cause bronchoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lower intracellular calcium tends to reduce, not increase, platelet activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insulin release requires calcium entry through L-type channels in beta cells, so blockade would reduce it.

questions.stem: These are the chemical structures of several calcium channel blockers grouped by structural class. Pharmacologically, the two non-dihydropyridine agents shown differ from the dihydropyridines by having a greater effect on which tissue?

explanation.summary: Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) act more strongly on cardiac conduction tissue, slowing SA/AV nodal firing (negative chronotropic/dromotropic effect), whereas dihydropyridines are relatively selective arterial vasodilators.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) act more strongly on cardiac conduction tissue, slowing SA/AV nodal firing (negative chronotropic/dromotropic effect), whereas dihydropyridines are relatively selective arterial vasodilators.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium channel blockers do not act preferentially on renal tubular epithelium; their main targets are vascular and cardiac tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchial smooth muscle is little affected by any calcium channel blocker class at therapeutic doses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Arteriolar smooth muscle is the preferred target of dihydropyridines like amlodipine and nifedipine, not of verapamil and diltiazem.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skeletal muscle contraction relies on sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium and is not meaningfully affected by either class.

questions.stem: This labeled schematic shows a motor-nerve action potential arriving at a skeletal muscle cell and triggering calcium handling across the sarcolemma, T-tubule, and internal calcium store. Loss of function of the L-type calcium channels (dihydropyridine receptors) depicted at the T-tubule would most directly reduce which downstream event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Potassium efflux from the muscle cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Repolarization of the motor nerve action potential

choices.label: C
choices.text: Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sodium influx through voltage-gated Na+ channels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acetylcholine release from the motor nerve terminal

explanation.summary: In skeletal muscle the T-tubule L-type channel (dihydropyridine receptor) acts mainly as a voltage sensor that is mechanically coupled to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1), so its depolarization-driven conformational change opens RyR1 and releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. (In cardiac muscle, Ca2+ entering through the channel instead triggers calcium-induced calcium release.) Upstream nerve signaling and Na+/K+ currents do not depend on this channel.
explanation.whyCorrect: In skeletal muscle the T-tubule L-type channel (dihydropyridine receptor) acts mainly as a voltage sensor that is mechanically coupled to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1), so its depolarization-driven conformational change opens RyR1 and releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. (In cardiac muscle, Ca2+ entering through the channel instead triggers calcium-induced calcium release.) Upstream nerve signaling and Na+/K+ currents do not depend on this channel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Potassium efflux drives repolarization of the muscle membrane and is not triggered by L-type calcium channels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The motor nerve action potential is presynaptic and upstream of the muscle's T-tubule calcium channels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sodium influx through muscle voltage-gated Na+ channels generates the depolarization that opens L-type channels, so it comes before them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acetylcholine release depends on presynaptic N- and P/Q-type calcium channels in the nerve terminal, not muscle L-type channels.
